Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Vignette:
Nguyen was a 31-year-old South Eastern Asian man married to his high school sweetheart. As a judge in one of the busiest courthouses in California, he spent most days navigating the complexities of legal proceedings and the emotional turmoil of those who came before him. However, beneath this composed exterior lay a deeply troubled psyche, shaped by the traumatic event that had shattered his sense of safety. A year ago, Nguyen and his wife were staying at their beach house during a particularly vicious storm season. The skies had been dark and foreboding for days, but they underestimated its ferocity until it was too late. When the floodwaters rushed into their home, everything changed in an instant. They barely made it to higher ground before their belongings were swept away, and Nguyen saw his wife struggle against the surging waters. The memory of that night haunted him daily. The sound of sirens from passing ambulances brought back a vivid sensory reliving of the terror he experienced. Each time he heard those wails, it was as if he could see the dark water rushing toward them, smell the antiseptic scent of emergency equipment, and feel the fear gripping his heart all over again. Nguyen's memories of that night were like snapshots—clear images etched in his mind, each a moment frozen in time. He saw himself pulling his wife to safety, feeling her weight and panic, hearing her cries for help. These images would often intrude during court sessions, leaving him distracted and anxious. To cope, he developed maladaptive strategies that only made things worse. Nguyen avoided relaxing because it felt dangerous; any moment of calmness brought a sudden jolt of fear as if the storm was about to return. He tried hard not to think about the trauma at all, but his efforts were futile. The images would come unbidden, and he found himself avoiding going out whenever possible. He feared that similar weather conditions might trigger another flood, leaving him trapped once again. As weeks turned into months, Nguyen's avoidance behaviors began to affect his daily life profoundly. His work as a judge suffered; he struggled to maintain focus during trials, often finding himself excusing himself to escape the sensory triggers or intrusive memories. This was especially challenging in courtrooms where the sterile scent of antiseptic lingered from recent cleaning. His wife noticed these changes but didn't fully understand what was driving them. She felt a growing distance between them as Nguyen's avoidance behaviors deepened their isolation. He had come to believe that going out and being relaxed were dangerous, so he avoided both at all costs. This belief made him feel trapped in his own home, unable to enjoy the simple pleasures of life. What frightened Nguyen most was the unpredictability of his memories. They could come at any time, turning a peaceful moment into one of intense fear and anxiety. He had tried to ignore these symptoms for months but eventually realized that he needed help. His work performance was suffering, and his marriage felt strained by his unexplained absences and avoidance. Seeking therapy became the only option he saw to regain control over his life. Nguyen hoped that through this process, he could find a way to manage his fears and memories without letting them dictate every aspect of his existence. He wanted to return to the judge he once was—a calm, composed figure who could handle the challenges of his profession with grace and confidence. In therapy, Nguyen expressed both fear and hope. Fear that he would never fully escape the haunting images from that stormy night, but also hope that with help, he could learn to live again without being constantly haunted by past trauma. The path forward was uncertain, but seeking help marked a crucial step toward reclaiming his life.
